newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. panel formally approves Iraq pricing formula.
newsitem.headline: U.N. panel formally approves Iraq pricing formula.

text.p: The U.N. Security Council sanctions committee on Iraq formally approved the December pricing formula for pending sales of Iraqi crude under the U.N. oil-for-food deal, diplomats said Wednesday.

U.S. objections had blocked adoption of pricing formulas in August and September. American protests were eliminated on Monday after Iraq unconditionally accepted terms of the May 20 accord, removing a key obstacle to allow Baghdad to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy food and aid for civilians suffering from sanctions imposed in 1990.
Diplomats said the Wednesday deadline for sanctions panel members to block the pricing formula expired with no objections, confirming expectations for certain approval.
The pricing formula dictates the terms of oil sales so that most contracts can be approved by the experts or overseers without going to the full sanctions committee.
Approval of the December plan, however, is not the final step in what has been an arduous process to bring Iraqi oil to world markets for the first time in six years.

Among the remaining tasks are an inspection of oil metering equipment on December 5 by the Dutch firm Saybolt to ensure faulty equipment at the Zakho station along the Iraq-Turkey border is operational. Lloyds Register personnel were also to inspect facilities this week, to ensure its ability to monitor aid imports.

Both companies were expected to report back to the United Nations by mid-December, giving U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali clearance to report the oil deal was ready for implementation before the end of the year.
Boutros-Ghali reported Wednesday to the U.N. Security Council that most arrangements for the oil-for-food deal were now in place, but did not say when the plan would start.
On Monday, Iraq's U.N. ambassador Nizar Hamdoon said he informed the United Nations of "the official Iraqi acceptance" of the terms of the May 20 Memorandum of Understanding.
Iraq had been insisting since mid-October that it control the number, makeup and freedom of movement of U.N. observers who would monitor arrangements on the ground, a stance the U.N. rejected.
Baghdad's acquiescense prompted Washington to drop its own policy of blocking the pricing formula adoption.
